Steven L. Lieberman 
Acting Under Secretary for Health 
Department of Veterans Affairs 
810 Vermont Avenue NW 
Washington, DC 20420 
 
RE:​
Reproductive Health Services; 38 CFR Part 17 (RIN 2900-AR57)  
 
Dear Steven Lieberman, Acting Under Secretary for Health: 
 
Planned Parenthood Federation of America (PPFA) submits this comment letter in response to the 
proposed rule, “Reproductive Health Services,” released by the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) on 
August 1, 2025 and published in the federal register on August 4, 2025. PPFA submits comments on 
proposals that would impact the overall health and well-being of the communities that Planned 
Parenthood members serve across the country. 
 
PPFA is a 501(c)(3) charitable organization that serves as the nation’s leading sexual and reproductive 
health care advocate and supports the independently incorporated Planned Parenthood members 
operating health centers (Planned Parenthood health centers) in communities across the United 
States. Planned Parenthood health centers  are trusted sources of healthcare for people of all 
1
genders, and they are also the nation’s largest sex educator and provider of information on healthy 
relationships. As a trusted advocate of sexual and reproductive health and national representative for 
Planned Parenthood health centers, PPFA strongly opposes the proposal to eliminate abortion and 
abortion counseling for veterans, their family members, and caregivers. 
 
Each year, Planned Parenthood health centers provide affordable birth control, lifesaving cancer 
screenings, testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections (STIs), abortion, and other 
essential care to more than two million patients and ensure that all people have accurate information 
about sexual and reproductive health. Notably, one in three women in the United States has been to a 
Planned Parenthood health center. The majority (65%) of Planned Parenthood patients have incomes 
at or below 150% of the Federal Poverty Level (FPL). 
 
It is our top priority to ensure that all individuals, including those receiving care through the VA health 
system, have the freedom to make their own informed health care decisions without interference from 
politicians, coercion, or barriers to the care they need. VA’s proposed rule would take away veterans’ 
1 Planned Parenthood health centers are 501(c)(3) charitable organizations. 
1 

 
autonomy and freedom over their bodies, lives, and futures, and it jeopardizes their long-term health 
and well-being. PPFA strongly urges VA to withdraw the proposed rule and provide comprehensive 
coverage for abortion and pregnancy options counseling to veterans and others eligible for VA medical 
benefits. At a minimum, VA should leave in place the current policy—which provides coverage for 
abortion counseling and abortion in cases of rape, incest, or where the life or health of the veteran is 
endangered. 
 
I.​
The abortion access crisis is an ongoing public health emergency, and the VA’s 
proposal to rescind this coverage for veterans and their dependents is reckless and 
dangerous.  
 
A.​ Abortion bans have harmed communities of color in particular, decreasing their health 
outcomes. 
 
Growing research shows that abortion bans have worsened maternal health outcomes in the United 
States, which already has higher rates of maternal death compared to other high-income countries.  
2
Women living in states that banned abortion are nearly two times as likely to die during pregnancy, 
childbirth, or soon after giving birth, compared to women living in states where abortion was legal and 
accessible.  
3
 
Communities of color are suffering the brunt of this crisis: Black women are 3.5 times more likely to 
experience a pregnancy-related death than white women,  and American Indian and Alaska Native 
4
women are more than twice as likely to experience a pregnancy-related death than white women.  In 
5
addition, researchers from Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health found that Black infants 
are dying at an 11% higher rate than would have been expected in the absence of abortion bans, and 
there are larger increases in infant mortality among both black infants and overall in Southern states.   
6

7

B.​ Veterans, including women veterans, face unique health care challenges that make access to 
abortion especially critical. 
 
There are more than two million women veterans in the United States, and they are the 
fastest-growing cohort of veterans; they are projected to make up 18% of all veterans by 2040.  
11
Nearly 300,000 women veterans who rely on the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) for care are of 
reproductive age.   
12
 
Women veterans have higher rates of pregnancy-related death and severe morbidity compared to 
non-veterans,  and Black veterans have 69% higher odds of any adverse event than those among 
13
white veterans.  Veterans of reproductive age, in particular, have high diagnosis rates of chronic 
14
mental health conditions—including depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)15
—that can increase the risks associated with pregnancy. 
 
Women veterans are at greater risk for serious mental health conditions like PTSD because they are 
more likely to experience certain traumatic events while deployed, such as direct combat and military

sexual trauma (MST).  For instance, among women Iraq and Afghanistan veterans, current VA data 
16
show that almost 20% have been diagnosed with PTSD.  
17
 
Finally, trans veterans and veterans with disabilities—many of whom need access to abortion—also 
experience other social barriers that make it harder to get care when they need it.  Trans veterans 
18
have higher rates of housing instability compared to cis veterans,  and more than 13% of veterans 
19
with disabilities have incomes below the federal poverty level, with higher prevalence in states that 
have banned abortion.  
20
 
C.​ The proposed rule will exacerbate the ongoing abortion access crisis and deepen the barriers 
veterans and their dependents face when trying to get an abortion. 
 
According to VA, over 155,000 veterans and nearly 50,000 CHAMPVA beneficiaries who may need 
abortion and rely on VA for health care live in states with abortion bans and restrictions.  As the 
21
largest health system in the United States, VHA is uniquely positioned to ensure that these veterans 
and their dependents receive timely abortion care no matter where they live, even in states that have 
enacted total or near total bans. 
 
Despite this, the proposed rule ignores VA’s vital role in providing abortion and counseling care by 
cruelly rolling back this coverage. Without abortion access through the VA, many veterans who need 
this care could be forced to travel to another state to reach a health care provider offering this care, or 
forgo this care entirely. Given the health risks veterans face, it is clear that they need to continue to 
have access to this essential care.  
 
II.​
VA’s proposed rule carves out just one narrow exception—life endangerment—leaving 
those with serious health risks and survivors of sexual assault without access to 
abortion or counseling.  
 
We know that even when there is an exception for the life of the pregnant person to an abortion ban, 
pregnant patients are denied critical, and sometimes lifesaving, medical care.  Providers are forced to 
22
prioritize consideration of the potential legal ramifications for providing care—rather than the health of

their patient—fearing punishment from state-sanctioned abortion bans.  This rule will similarly narrow 
23
the care available to veterans and could delay care until patients are on the brink of death and exclude 
those with serious health risks.  
 
The proposed rule additionally excludes those who are survivors of rape and incest. Dr. Toni Marengo, 
MD, FACOG—a Navy veteran and Chief Medical Transformation Officer at Planned Parenthood of the 
Pacific Southwest—emphasized how harmful the proposed rule is: 
 
The statistics are stark: one in three women veterans report experiencing sexual trauma in the 
military. Women and LGBTQ+ veterans face a higher risk of sexual assault and intimate 
partner violence. Denying them access to abortion care is not only unjust – it is dangerous. 
Restricting access to abortion care forces veterans to travel long distances, pay out of pocket, 
and use limited time off, creating unnecessary barriers to essential medical services. This 
directly undermines their ability to make informed decisions about their own health and bodies, 
and eliminates their ability to exercise the very rights they fight to protect.  
24
 
PPFA reminds the VA that the majority of sexual assault incidences are unreported. Significant 
burdens and requirements needed to prove rape or incest can dissuade survivors of this violence from 
reporting the offense.  Stigma and shame, as well as fear of retaliation from their abuser, can also 
25
discourage individuals from reporting or receiving the medical testing that is often required to confirm 
rape or incest has occurred.  This makes the proposed rule all the more egregious, as it will take 
26
away essential care from people who face immense obstacles in getting an abortion. 
 
Finally, PPFA notes the proposed rule seeks only to make the life endangerment exception explicit in 
the regulatory text for the CHAMPVA program, but not the VA medical benefits package. If the agency 
is to proceed forward with finalizing this proposed rule, at a minimum, VA must include the life 
endangerment exception in the VA regulations. 
 
III.​
VA’s proposed rule will further decrease access to care for veterans that live in rural 
states. 
 
The ten states with the highest proportion of veterans are: Alaska (11% share of adult population); 
Virginia, Montana, and Wyoming (9% of share); and South Carolina, Maine, South Dakota, Oklahoma,

27
Alaska, which has the most veterans per capita —these states will be especially harmed by the 
28
proposed rule. 
 
Many of these states are primarily rural and already face significant health care infrastructure issues 
that make it harder for veterans to get care. For example, nearly 290,000 Alaskans live in a primary 
care health professional shortage area, and the state has approximately one fifth of the number of 
primary care providers required to adequately serve its overall population.  U.S. Senator Lisa 
29
Murkowski (R-AK) described the hurdles Alaskan veterans experience in getting health care in a 
recent hearing discussing the Department of Veterans Affairs’ Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26) budget request, 
“Everything from traveling the long distances…trying to access them through telehealth, but when you 
have limited broadband, that’s a problem. Then we have shortages of local health care providers. It’s 
complicated in many ways, but all of our veterans deserve this care.”  
30
 
IV.​
Abortion counseling allows veterans to make informed decisions about their own 
bodies, health, and well-being.  
 
The proposed rule’s banning VA providers from comprehensive pregnancy counseling imposes an 
unconscionable “gag” rule on the health care that veterans can receive. The proposed “gag” rule would 
interfere with a provider’s ability and ethical responsibility to offer their patients the full range of 
medical options and would make it impossible for pregnant veterans to make fully informed decisions 
about their health and bodies. As VA noted in the September 2022 IFR, abortion counseling “is a 
component of comprehensive, patient-centered, high quality reproductive health care both as a 
responsibility of the provider and a right of the pregnant veteran.”  Pregnant patients deserve to have 
31
the information they need about all of their health care options—including abortion.  
 
Prohibiting pregnant veterans from receiving counseling on abortion denies those who have sacrificed 
and served the United States their own reproductive freedom. VA must withdraw this cruel provision, 
which serves no purposes but to harm veterans’ health and well-being. 
  
V.​
Combined with the VA’s ban on gender-affirming care, this rule further singles out 
veterans and denies them lifesaving care.

VA is a major provider of gender-affirming care in this country. However, effective March 17, 2025, VA 
stopped providing hormone therapy for gender dysphoria to veterans, with narrow exceptions.  In the 
32
same announcement, VA also affirmed that veterans could not receive gender-affirming surgery in any 
circumstance, continuing the longstanding ban on this care. 
 
Independent studies consistently show that trans people who receive medically necessary health care 
like hormone therapy have better mental health outcomes.  Coupled with the ongoing 
33
gender-affirming care ban, the proposed rule’s ban on abortion care denies veterans the right to 
access essential medical services and continues to place veterans at a disadvantage—further risking 
their health and well-being. 
 
***** 
Planned Parenthood Federation of America strongly urges the Department of Veterans Affairs to put 
the health and lives of veterans and their family members—including women, people of color, people 
with disabilities, and LGBTQ+ communities—first and foremost, and to work towards fulfilling, rather 
than undermining, VA’s responsibility to provide medically determined care that is needed to “promote, 
preserve, or restore the health”  of the veterans it serves. This includes ensuring access to abortion 
34
without political interference. 
 
The proposed rule runs counter to VA’s responsibility and dangerously eliminates essential health 
coverage that veterans and their family members need. For these reasons, VA should withdraw the 
proposed rule and provide comprehensive coverage for abortion and pregnancy options counseling; at 
a minimum, VA should leave the current policy in place. 
 
Our comments include numerous citations to supporting research, including direct links to the 
research, for VA’s benefit in reviewing our comments. We direct VA to each of the studies cited and 
made available to the agency through active hyperlinks, and we request that the full text of each of the 
studies cited, along with the full text of our comments, be considered part of the administrative record 
in this matter for purposes of the Administrative Procedure Act. 
 
Respectfully, 
Laurel Sakai
